title: What are the common SQL string functions — `CONCAT` / `||`, `SUBSTRING` / `SUBSTR`, `LENGTH` / `CHAR_LENGTH`, `TRIM` / `LTRIM` / `RTRIM`, `UPPER` / `LOWER`, `REPLACE`, `POSITION` / `INSTR`, `LEFT` / `RIGHT`, `LPAD` / `RPAD`, `REVERSE` — and how does syntax vary across MySQL / PostgreSQL / Oracle?
shortTitle: Common SQL string functions and cross-database syntax differences

s1_definition.profdef: SQL string functions transform and inspect character data inside the database: concatenation, substring extraction, length, trimming whitespace, case conversion, search-and-replace, position lookup, padding, and reversal. The exact names and operators differ across MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle, so portable code either sticks to the SQL-standard forms or abstracts the differences.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India prints a statement, it must format Rajesh's name as "RAJESH KUMAR", mask his account to "XXXX2001", trim stray spaces from imported data, and build display strings like "SAV2001 - Rajesh". String functions are the bank's text toolbox for cleaning and formatting customer data.
s1_definition.oneliner: String functions clean, format, and inspect text — but check the dialect, because Oracle's SUBSTR and MySQL's CONCAT differ from PostgreSQL's || operator.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SQL string functions transform and inspect character data inside the database: concatenation, substring extraction, length, trimming whitespace, case conversion, search-and-replace, position lookup, padding, and reversal. The exact names and operators differ across MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle, so portable code either sticks to the SQL-standard forms or abstracts the differences.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India prints a statement, it must format Rajesh's name as "RAJESH KUMAR", mask his account to "XXXX2001", trim stray spaces from imported data, and build display strings like "SAV2001 - Rajesh". String functions are the bank's text toolbox for cleaning and formatting customer data.

**One line to remember:** String functions clean, format, and inspect text — but check the dialect, because Oracle's SUBSTR and MySQL's CONCAT differ from PostgreSQL's || operator.

sections.s2_technical:
Concatenation: PostgreSQL and Oracle use `'a' || 'b'`; MySQL uses `CONCAT('a','b')` (its `||` is logical OR unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT is set). Example: `SELECT id || ' - ' || holder FROM accounts` gives "SAV2001 - Rajesh Kumar" on PostgreSQL.

Substring: standard `SUBSTRING(str FROM 2 FOR 3)`; MySQL/Oracle also accept `SUBSTR(str, 2, 3)`. Example masking: `'XXXX' || RIGHT(id, 4)`.

Length: `LENGTH` counts characters in PostgreSQL/Oracle and bytes in MySQL, so use `CHAR_LENGTH` in MySQL for character count. Trim: `TRIM(str)`, `LTRIM`, `RTRIM`; standard `TRIM(BOTH ' ' FROM str)`. Case: `UPPER`, `LOWER`. Replace: `REPLACE(str, from, to)`. Position: `POSITION('x' IN str)` (standard), `INSTR(str,'x')` (MySQL/Oracle). LEFT/RIGHT exist in MySQL and PostgreSQL; Oracle uses SUBSTR with negative offsets. Padding: `LPAD(id, 10, '0')`, `RPAD`. Reverse: `REVERSE`.

Senior nuance: wrapping an indexed column in a function, like `WHERE UPPER(holder) = 'RAJESH'`, defeats a plain index. Either store a normalized column, add a functional index on `UPPER(holder)`, or use case-insensitive collation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India imports account data from a legacy file with inconsistent spacing and casing, and the statement screen needs masked account numbers and a clean display label. This is exactly what string functions do: trim, upper-case, mask, and concatenate.

The demo has a `StatementFormatter` with methods `displayLabel()`, `maskAccount()`, and `normalizeName()`, mirroring the SQL functions, plus a runner formatting Rajesh's and Priya's details.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
statement-format-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/bank/strfn/
    ├── StringFnDemo.java
    └── service/StatementFormatter.java
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__string_fns.sql (demonstrates the functions per dialect)
-- PostgreSQL / Oracle concatenation with ||
SELECT id || ' - ' || holder AS label FROM accounts;      -- "SAV2001 - Rajesh Kumar"
-- MySQL concatenation
SELECT CONCAT(id, ' - ', holder) AS label FROM accounts;
-- Masking last 4: standard RIGHT / SUBSTR
SELECT 'XXXX' || RIGHT(id, 4) AS masked FROM accounts;    -- "XXXX2001"
-- Normalize imported name
SELECT UPPER(TRIM(holder)) AS clean FROM accounts;        -- "RAJESH KUMAR"
-- Position of a separator
SELECT POSITION('-' IN label) FROM (SELECT id||'-'||holder label FROM accounts) q;
-- Zero-pad a numeric id
SELECT LPAD(CAST(seq AS VARCHAR), 8, '0') FROM txns;      -- "00000042"
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: id "SAV2001" and a messy imported name "  rajesh kumar " with leading/trailing spaces and lower case.

Step 1: normalizeName trims the spaces and upper-cases, giving "RAJESH KUMAR" — same as SQL `UPPER(TRIM(holder))`.

Step 2: displayLabel concatenates id, " - ", and the cleaned name, like SQL `id || ' - ' || UPPER(TRIM(holder))`.

Step 3: maskAccount takes the last four characters of "CUR3001" and prefixes XXXX.

```text
2026-10-25 18:16:00 [INFO] displayLabel -> SAV2001 - RAJESH KUMAR
SAV2001 - RAJESH KUMAR
masked: XXXX3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  raw: id="SAV2001", holder="  rajesh kumar "
    │
    ▼  TRIM + UPPER  ──→ "RAJESH KUMAR"
    │
    ▼  id || ' - ' || name  ──→ "SAV2001 - RAJESH KUMAR"
    │
    ▼  'XXXX' || RIGHT(id,4) ──→ "XXXX3001"
    ▼
  formatted statement line
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — StatementFormatter ═══

  ┌─ SOLID S: formatter only formats text; no persistence ─┐
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     StatementFormatter       │
  │  + displayLabel(id,holder)   │  SQL: ||  / CONCAT
  │  + maskAccount(id)           │  SQL: RIGHT / SUBSTR
  │  + normalizeName(holder)     │  SQL: UPPER(TRIM())
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Dialect note: || (PG/Oracle) vs CONCAT (MySQL);
                LENGTH bytes in MySQL → use CHAR_LENGTH.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The common SQL string functions cover concatenation, substring extraction, length, trimming, case conversion, replacement, position lookup, left and right slicing, padding, and reversal. The key senior point is that the dialects differ: PostgreSQL and Oracle concatenate with the double-pipe operator while MySQL uses the CONCAT function and treats double-pipe as logical OR by default; Oracle and MySQL offer SUBSTR while the standard is SUBSTRING; and MySQL's LENGTH counts bytes so I use CHAR_LENGTH there for character counts.

In our National Bank of India statement service I used these constantly — I normalized messy imported names with UPPER and TRIM, built display labels by concatenating the account id, a separator, and the cleaned name, masked account numbers by prefixing XXXX to the right-most four characters, and zero-padded sequence numbers with LPAD. The one performance trap I always call out is that wrapping an indexed column in a function, such as filtering on UPPER of the holder name, defeats a normal index, so I either store a normalized column, create a functional index on the expression, or use a case-insensitive collation. The line I remember is that string functions clean, format, and inspect text, but I always confirm the dialect because the concatenation operator and the substring and length names genuinely differ across databases.
